paragraphs: Programming by example asks a system to infer a program from examples of inputs and their desired outputs. The system searches for a combination of available base functions that produces those transformations. This can be difficult because many combinations are possible, and the examples alone do not directly specify which components to try.

The paper uses machine learning to guide that search. It learns weights connecting textual features of the input-output examples with plausible program components. Those connections provide a way to use information in the examples when searching for candidate programs and ranking them. The contribution is a generic learning framework that can address problems beyond the scope of earlier programming-by-example systems.

Experiments with a prototype cover several text-processing tasks drawn from help forums. The reported results show improvements in both search and ranking when learning is used. These findings support the idea that learned associations between examples and program components can make program inference more effective on practical text-processing problems.
icml-2013-a-machine-learning-framework-f.tldr: Learning relationships between input-output examples and program components improves the search for text-processing programs.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a Gaussian graphical model while deciding how sparse its precision matrix should be. A common approach places a sparsity-promoting prior, such as a Laplace prior, on matrix entries. That approach requires choosing a hyperparameter that controls the amount of sparsity, making this choice part of the estimation problem.

The proposed method makes sparsity adapt automatically to the data through a hierarchical Bayesian model. It uses a non-informative Jeffreys’ hyperprior to avoid a separately tuned sparsity parameter. The precision matrix is represented through a Cholesky decomposition, which naturally enforces the symmetry and positive-definiteness constraints that a valid precision matrix must satisfy.

Experiments use both simulated data and real cell-signaling data. The method automatically adjusts sparsity and produces better precision-matrix estimates than the compared Laplace-prior model, whose sparsity parameter is selected by cross-validation. The findings therefore support both parts of the proposal: removing manual sparsity tuning and improving estimation in the evaluated settings.
icml-2013-adaptive-sparsity-in-gaussian-.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model automatically adapts precision-matrix sparsity and improves estimates in simulated and cell-signaling experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decisions in which an action combines several simpler uncertain choices. These combined actions are called super arms. Playing one reveals outcomes of its related simple arms, providing information for later decisions. The framework permits many nonlinear reward structures, provided the reward satisfies two stated mild assumptions.

The method also assumes access to an approximation oracle. Given the simple arms’ mean outcomes, this oracle returns an action achieving an alpha fraction of the optimal expected reward with probability beta. Performance is measured using approximation regret: the reward shortfall relative to an alpha-times-beta fraction of the reward from always choosing the optimal super arm.

The proposed CUCB algorithm has logarithmic regret in the number of rounds under the framework, and the paper also provides distribution-independent bounds for a broad class of rewards. Its analysis matches the classical bandit bound up to a constant factor. Applications to probabilistic advertising coverage and social influence maximization demonstrate the framework’s relevance to nonlinear decision problems.
icml-2013-combinatorial-multi-armed-band.tldr: CUCB provides logarithmic approximation regret for a broad combinatorial bandit framework that includes nonlinear rewards.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers a classifier from a labeled source domain to a different target domain without target labels. The paper addresses this problem by learning features intended to remain useful across domains. Its central observation is that some labeled source examples may already have a distribution particularly similar to the target data.

The method automatically identifies these source examples as landmarks. It uses them to construct auxiliary adaptation tasks that are provably easier, creating intermediate connections between the source and target. Solutions to those tasks then become the ingredients for features used in the original adaptation problem. The composition of those features is optimized discriminatively without requiring labeled target examples.

Experiments evaluate the approach on benchmark tasks involving visual object recognition and text sentiment analysis. The reported results significantly outperform the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a way to make source-to-target transfer more manageable by exploiting relevant subsets of source data and combining the resulting auxiliary solutions.
icml-2013-connecting-the-dots-with-landm.tldr: Automatically discovered source landmarks support easier adaptation tasks whose solutions form useful features without target labels.

paragraphs: When an SVM is learned together with a linear transformation of its features, the transformation changes the spread of the data. Consequently, the radius of the smallest sphere enclosing the data is no longer fixed. The paper argues that accounting for both this radius and the classification margin has the potential to tighten the SVM error bound.

It introduces two algorithms: one for feature selection and another for metric learning. Both directly optimize a radius-margin error bound using linear transformations. Their construction combines a tighter approximation of the radius with a metric-learning interpretation of SVMs. The resulting optimization problems are convex quadratic problems with linear or quadratic constraints, unlike most existing radius-margin formulations.

Benchmark experiments report strong feature-selection performance against methods including L1 and elastic-net approaches. The metric-learning variant significantly improves classification relative to the compared SVM methods. These results support incorporating data spread into the learning objective, alongside the margin, in the evaluated settings.
icml-2013-convex-formulations-of-radius-.tldr: Two convex SVM formulations jointly account for data radius and margin, improving feature selection and classification in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: In large-scale applications, a classifier must fit within a prediction-time computing budget as well as make accurate decisions. The paper focuses on feature extraction, which often dominates this cost. Different features can require very different amounts of computation, so treating every input with the same feature set can make prediction unnecessarily expensive.

The proposed approach arranges classifiers in a tree. Each test input follows an individual path, and different paths extract different features. A path is optimized for a particular region of the input space, allowing the system to tailor its computation to the kinds of inputs reaching that path. Feature-extraction time is explicitly incorporated into this design.

The underlying idea is to compute features for the inputs that benefit from them most. The paper reports that this cost-sensitive tree can match the high accuracy of contemporary state-of-the-art methods at a small fraction of their computational cost. Its contribution is a principled way to balance prediction accuracy with the expense of obtaining the information needed for a decision.
icml-2013-cost-sensitive-tree-of-classif.tldr: A tree of classifiers selectively computes features for each input, matching high accuracy at substantially lower prediction cost.

paragraphs: Sharing an intermediate representation across prediction tasks can save computation, but compressing that representation may reduce accuracy. Earlier sparselets provided such a shared representation for multiclass object detection and delivered substantial speedups accompanied by a large loss in task performance. This paper revisits how the active parts of that representation are learned.

The proposed training framework learns which sparselets to activate by optimizing a discriminative objective tied to prediction. It first expresses sparselets within a general structured-output framework, then analyzes when they yield computational savings. This connects the choice of active sparselets to the task being solved and broadens the formulation beyond the original object-detection setting.

Experiments cover object detection and image classification. They show that discriminative activation substantially outperforms the earlier reconstructive approach, with larger speedups and no decrease in task performance in the reported results. The findings indicate that compression and efficient sharing can work better when the selection of representation components is trained for the final predictive task.
icml-2013-discriminatively-activated-spa.tldr: Learning sparselet activations for prediction yields larger speedups without the performance loss reported for earlier sparselets.

paragraphs: The paper addresses domain adaptation for sequence labeling: using language-processing systems across different data domains. Its approach learns distributed representations that can supply useful information to these systems. The representations are designed to encode both latent features that generalize between domains and features specific to an individual domain.

A log-bilinear neural probabilistic language adaptation model jointly represents the two related distributions in the source and target domains. The resulting dense, real-valued representations are added as features to language-processing systems. This makes the learned representation the mechanism for adaptation, connecting joint modeling of the domains to the information available for sequence-labeling decisions.

The empirical evaluation covers part-of-speech tagging on WSJ and MEDLINE, and syntactic chunking and named-entity recognition on WSJ and Brown corpora. The primary results outperform several comparison methods on cross-domain labeling tasks. These findings support using representations that retain domain-specific information while also learning information that can transfer between the source and target.
icml-2013-domain-adaptation-for-sequence.tldr: A joint language model learns transferable and domain-specific features that improve cross-domain sequence labeling in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Dynamic social-network models often explain observed interactions through hidden structure that changes over time. This paper focuses on another part of that relationship: how previously observed social relationships affect the network’s future hidden structure. It calls this phenomenon latent feature propagation, emphasizing the role of past connections in the evolution of unobserved network features.

The authors introduce a probabilistic model that captures this temporal relationship. The modeling target therefore includes how observed relationships from the past inform latent structure at later times. This matters because a model of network evolution can use social relationships as information about how hidden structure develops, as well as explain interactions through that structure.

The paper demonstrates inference of latent structure across different types of social-network datasets. Experiments report higher predictive performance for link prediction and forecasting using the inferred structure. The results support the predictive usefulness of modeling latent feature propagation in the evaluated data, connecting the proposed account of network evolution to improvements on future-relationship prediction tasks.
icml-2013-dynamic-probabilistic-models-f.tldr: Modeling how past social relationships shape future latent features improves link prediction and forecasting in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Some high-dimensional learning problems require selecting useful individual features while also identifying relevant groups of features. The paper addresses these two decisions together through sparse group feature selection. It explores a nonconvex approach because commonly used convex methods may be suboptimal for selecting features accurately and estimating their associated parameters.

The computational contribution is a nonconvex model and an efficient optimization algorithm. A central step projects onto a set defined by two coupled constraints, reflecting the need to handle the selection requirements jointly. The statistical contribution is a result showing that the proposed model can reconstruct an oracle estimator, supporting the possibility of consistent feature selection and parameter estimation.

Numerical experiments use both synthetic and real-world data. Their results suggest favorable performance relative to competing methods. The paper thus combines an algorithmic proposal with a statistical recovery result: it aims to make nonconvex sparse group selection computationally practical while showing how the model can support accurate recovery, beyond the empirical comparisons alone.
icml-2013-efficient-sparse-group-feature.tldr: A nonconvex sparse group selection method combines efficient optimization with an oracle-recovery result and favorable numerical comparisons.

paragraphs: Non-negative matrix factorization becomes tractable under a structural condition called separability. This paper works within that setting and develops a geometric reformulation. It views the factorization problem as finding the extreme rays of the conical hull formed by a finite collection of vectors, turning the task into one of identifying the defining directions of that cone.

This geometric viewpoint leads to new algorithms for separable non-negative matrix factorization. The authors report that the methods are highly scalable and empirically robust to noise, with several favorable properties relative to existing approaches. Separability is central to the formulation, while the reported noise robustness describes how the algorithms behave in experiments.

The paper also presents a parallel implementation that scales well on both shared-memory and distributed-memory machines. This makes scalability a practical part of the contribution, alongside the geometric formulation. Together, the results show how exploiting the structure of separable factorization can produce algorithms suited to larger computations while retaining useful empirical behavior in the presence of noise.
icml-2013-fast-conical-hull-algorithms-f.tldr: A geometric reformulation of separable non-negative matrix factorization yields scalable algorithms with empirical noise robustness and effective parallelization.

paragraphs: Structured labeling requires predictions that capture relationships among labels. Layered approaches address this by passing information through sequences of classifiers or regressors, but learning multiple different models across layers creates an additional burden. This paper proposes a fixed-point model as a simpler way to capture the contextual information needed for structured prediction.

The key idea is to learn a function that takes structured labels as input and also produces structured labels as output. The desired labeling is represented through a fixed point of that function. The paper develops a training strategy and provides justifications for the function to be a contraction mapping, giving mathematical support to the proposed fixed-point formulation.

The learned function captures rich context while being easy to train and evaluate, according to the paper. Experiments on several widely used benchmarks report significant improvements in both predictive performance and efficiency over many compared methods. These findings support organizing structured labeling around a learned fixed-point function while reducing the burden of training separate models for different layers.
icml-2013-fixed-point-model-for-structur.tldr: A learned fixed-point function captures label context and improves structured-labeling performance and efficiency on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: Supervised topic models connect latent topics with prediction tasks. Existing max-margin versions use an iterative procedure that repeatedly solves latent SVM subproblems and imposes mean-field assumptions on posterior distributions. This paper develops an alternative formulation intended to simplify that inference procedure for both classification and regression.

The proposed models minimize an expected margin loss. This objective upper-bounds the existing margin loss derived from an expected prediction rule, establishing a relationship between the new formulation and the earlier one. By introducing augmented variables, the authors obtain simple Gibbs sampling algorithms that avoid solving SVM subproblems and remove the restrictive posterior assumptions described for the existing approach.

Experiments show significant improvements in time efficiency. Classification performance also improves significantly over the compared methods. The results indicate that changing the loss formulation and introducing auxiliary sampling variables can improve both computation and classification in these supervised topic models. The algorithmic framework covers regression as well, while the abstract’s explicit predictive-performance improvement concerns classification.
icml-2013-gibbs-max-margin-topic-models-.tldr: An expected-margin formulation enables fast Gibbs sampling for supervised topic models and improves classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Fast nearest-neighbor retrieval depends on representing data so that useful proximity relationships remain easy to search. This paper learns hash functions from triplets expressing relative proximity: which of two points should be closer to another. The objective is to preserve these comparisons as well as possible in compact binary representations.

The proposed method, CGHash, uses a large-margin learning framework and implements learning through column generation. Each iteration selects the best hash function for that step. Its training objective is convex, allowing a global optimum to be identified. The learned functions also apply naturally to new data points, extending the representation beyond the examples used during training.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets show that CGHash learns compact binary codes and compares favorably with state-of-the-art retrieval methods. The contribution connects relative comparison information to an optimization procedure for constructing hash functions. The findings support the usefulness of this combination for retrieval, while the convex formulation provides a separate optimization property beyond the empirical results.
icml-2013-learning-hash-functions-using-.tldr: CGHash uses column generation and relative proximity comparisons to learn compact binary codes through a convex training objective.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning linear Bayesian networks when some variables cannot be observed. The goal is to recover information about the network using the variables that are available. This raises two distinct questions: whether the observable information can identify the underlying network, and whether that recovery can be carried out efficiently.

The authors establish identifiability and efficient recovery from low-order observable moments under a new graphical constraint. That constraint concerns expansion properties of the directed acyclic graph connecting observed and unobserved variables. The result therefore ties recoverability to the network’s connection structure and shows that low-order summaries of observable data can suffice under that condition.

The constraint is satisfied by many natural graph families, including multi-level directed acyclic graphs, graphs with effective depth one, and certain polytrees. This breadth matters because the condition applies across several kinds of network organization. The central contribution is a conditional recovery guarantee: hidden variables can be accommodated efficiently when the underlying graph has the required expansion properties.
icml-2013-learning-linear-bayesian-netwo.tldr: A graphical expansion condition enables identifiable, efficient recovery of linear Bayesian networks with hidden variables from low-order observable moments.

paragraphs: This paper studies training support vector machines with a guarantee on how many support vectors the learned model uses. Its target is sparsity in the support-vector representation. The central claim is that the number of support vectors can be made optimal up to constant factors, giving a formal guarantee on this aspect of the learned model.

The guarantee is paired with bounds on sample complexity and training time that match the best known bounds for kernel SVM optimization. In asymptotic terms, the proposed method achieves its support-vector guarantee without adding cost beyond standard SVM training. This combination matters because a sparse result is obtained together with competitive bounds on the resources needed to learn it.

The authors also describe the method as simple to implement and report that it works well in practice. The main contribution combines three properties: support-vector sparsity with an optimality guarantee up to constants, established learning and runtime bounds, and practical usability. The abstract presents these as compatible features of one training method.
icml-2013-learning-optimally-sparse-supp.tldr: The method trains SVMs with an optimal support-vector count up to constants without additional asymptotic sample or training cost.

paragraphs: Computer-vision performance often depends heavily on configuration choices that researchers tune by hand. Those choices may need to change for each domain, and the process can depend on experience that is difficult to describe or reproduce. This makes it hard to separate the quality of an algorithm from the quality of its tuning.

The paper proposes a meta-modeling framework for automated hyperparameter optimization. It exposes an expression graph describing how hyperparameters lead to a performance metric, such as validation accuracy. The parameters govern both the behavior of processing steps and which steps are included. An optimization algorithm transforms this graph into a program that searches for configurations improving the metric.

Using one broad family of feed-forward vision architectures, the approach achieves reported state-of-the-art results on LFW face verification, PubFig83 face identification, and CIFAR-10 object recognition. These results show the reach of automated configuration across different vision tasks. The broader aim is a reproducible, unbiased optimization process that makes model search an explicit part of evaluating an approach.
icml-2013-making-a-science-of-model-sear.tldr: An expression-graph framework automates vision architecture tuning and achieves reported state-of-the-art results on three distinct tasks.

paragraphs: Maximum Variance Unfolding is a manifold-learning method whose embeddings have potential applications in search. This paper introduces Maximum Variance Correction, or MVC, to make feasible MVU solutions available at much larger scales. The method works by post-processing embeddings produced by any manifold-learning algorithm, making correction of an existing embedding the central computational step.

The authors report that MVC increases the scale of MVU embeddings by several orders of magnitude and is naturally parallel. This scalability matters for applications that require embeddings large enough to represent substantial search problems. The paper specifically explores using MVU embeddings as heuristics to accelerate A* search, connecting a geometric representation to a search procedure.

Experiments on several nontrivial A* benchmark problems report reductions in search time unmatched in the comparisons presented. The contribution links a scalable embedding procedure with a concrete downstream use. MVC’s large-scale feasible solutions make it possible to investigate manifold-learning embeddings as practical aids to search, and the reported benchmarks demonstrate substantial benefits for that application.
icml-2013-maximum-variance-correction-wi.tldr: MVC scales feasible Maximum Variance Unfolding embeddings through post-processing and uses them to substantially accelerate benchmark A* searches.

paragraphs: Learning a dynamical-system model is especially difficult when observations are high-dimensional and only reveal part of the system. This paper introduces Compressed Predictive State Representation, or CPSR, for learning such models from small sample sets. Its stated setting is partially observable, uncontrolled dynamical systems, including domains with extremely large discrete observation spaces.

CPSR extends predictive state representations by exploiting a particular sparse structure found in many domains. That structure allows information to be compressed during learning, improving efficiency and predictive power. The compression also reduces the burden of selecting domain-specific features, making the approach relevant when constructing a manageable representation by hand would be difficult.

Empirical results show that CPSR builds accurate models more efficiently than uncompressed counterparts. The paper also provides theoretical results concerning the accuracy of the compressed model. Together, these contributions support compression as a useful part of learning when the relevant sparse structure is present, with both experimental evidence and mathematical analysis addressing the quality of the resulting predictions.
icml-2013-modelling-sparse-dynamical-sys.tldr: CPSR exploits sparse structure to learn accurate compressed models of high-dimensional partially observed systems more efficiently.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the top m arms in a multi-armed bandit problem. The desired output is a collection of strong choices, so the algorithm must distinguish which candidates belong in that collection. The authors develop a selection procedure that makes progress by deciding both which arms to discard and which to retain.

Their algorithm combines successive rejection of arms that appear poor with successive acceptance of arms that appear good. These two kinds of decisions address opposite sides of the identification task. Rejection removes seemingly unsuitable candidates, while acceptance commits to promising ones. The contribution is this combined algorithmic approach to identifying multiple arms.

The authors show that the same idea also applies to best-arm identification across multiple bandit problems. They describe this extension as enabling multiple-identification settings that earlier approaches could not handle. The significance is therefore broader than selecting a top-m set in one game: successive acceptance and rejection provides a reusable strategy for several related identification tasks.
icml-2013-multiple-identifications-in-mu.tldr: Successively accepting promising arms and rejecting poor ones supports top-m selection and best-arm identification across multiple bandits.

paragraphs: Active learning can reduce labeling effort by selecting informative examples, but practical systems often need to request several labels at once. Batch requests allow parallel work in settings such as crowdsourcing and experimental design. The paper examines the theoretical quality of batch decisions, addressing a gap left by previously proposed heuristics.

The analysis covers batch active learning and more general stochastic optimization problems with adaptive submodularity, a diminishing-returns condition. For these problems, the authors prove that a simple greedy strategy is competitive with the optimal batch policy. In some cases, batch decisions also incur competitively low cost when compared with a fully sequential strategy that receives feedback between decisions.

Experiments demonstrate the approach on batch active-learning tasks, where it outperforms the compared state of the art, and on multi-stage influence maximization in social networks. The contribution combines conditional performance guarantees with empirical evidence. It shows that parallel information gathering can have a strong theoretical basis when the problem exhibits the required diminishing-returns structure.
icml-2013-near-optimal-batch-mode-active.tldr: Under adaptive submodularity, a greedy batch strategy competes with optimal batch policies and sometimes compares favorably with sequential decisions.

paragraphs: Dirichlet-process mixture models are useful when the number of underlying components is unknown, but inference can be slow. Distributing the computation offers a route to larger problems. The difficulty addressed here is that earlier attempts at parallel inference introduced approximations that could reduce the accuracy of the estimated posterior distribution.

The paper develops auxiliary-variable representations for both the Dirichlet process and the hierarchical Dirichlet process. These representations allow Markov chain Monte Carlo computation to be distributed while retaining the correct equilibrium distribution. The key contribution is therefore a way to reorganize inference across computing resources while preserving the distribution that the sampling procedure is intended to target.

The authors report scalable inference without the deterioration in estimate quality associated with the existing approaches they discuss. This matters because computational scale and posterior fidelity are addressed together. The equilibrium-distribution result supports the correctness of the sampling target, while the reported scalability shows why the representation is useful for performing inference in these nonparametric mixture models.
icml-2013-parallel-markov-chain-monte-ca.tldr: Auxiliary-variable representations enable distributed MCMC for Dirichlet-process models while preserving the correct equilibrium distribution.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes Copula Component Analysis, a semiparametric form of principal component analysis, when observations are dependent. Its model assumes that unspecified monotone transformations of individual variables yield a multivariate Gaussian distribution. This permits non-Gaussian observed data while retaining a structured model after transformation.

The analysis considers both m-dependent observations and the more general phi-mixing setting. It establishes convergence bounds for support recovery and parameter estimation, showing that COCA can tolerate weak dependence. The authors also provide explicit sufficient conditions on the degree of dependence under which the parametric convergence rate is maintained. These are conditions guaranteeing the rate, rather than a claim about arbitrary dependence.

The results extend the earlier analysis of COCA to dependent observations in high-dimensional settings. This broadens the theoretical circumstances in which the method is supported, covering data that do not satisfy an independent-observation assumption. The authors also identify their proof techniques as potentially useful for studying other multivariate statistical methods, beyond this particular principal-component procedure.
icml-2013-principal-component-analysis-o.tldr: COCA retains theoretical recovery guarantees under weak dependence, with sufficient conditions for maintaining the parametric convergence rate.

paragraphs: Structured-output prediction can be approached through regression, but a good regression fit needs a mathematical connection to the prediction loss that ultimately matters. This paper supplies guarantees for that connection. It studies quadratic regression loss as a tractable training objective for predicting structured outputs.

The authors show that quadratic regression loss is a convex surrogate for prediction loss when the output kernel satisfies a condition relating it to that loss. They then derive two upper bounds on prediction risk, each depending on the predictor’s empirical quadratic risk. These bounds link performance on the regression objective measured from data to control of the structured-prediction risk.

Minimizing the first bound recovers a previously proposed predictor, while minimizing the second produces a new one. The paper compares both predictors on practical tasks. Its contribution therefore has two parts: a conditional theoretical justification for the regression approach and a way to derive learning algorithms from different risk bounds. The abstract reports the comparison without declaring either predictor the empirical winner.
icml-2013-risk-bounds-and-learning-algor.tldr: Conditional risk bounds justify quadratic regression for structured prediction and yield both an existing predictor and a new one.

paragraphs: Linear classifiers are efficient to train and evaluate, while nonlinear methods can provide more expressive decision rules at greater computational cost. Explicit feature embeddings offer a way to combine nonlinear representations with linear learning, but their construction can be expensive and their accuracy can fall below kernel methods. This paper proposes a different nonlinear feature map.

The map discretizes and interpolates individual feature values and pairs of features. Discretization lets different regions of feature space be modeled separately, while interpolation preserves the original continuous values. The resulting representation is strictly more general than a linear model and is reported to be as efficient as an explicit second-order polynomial feature map.

An extensive empirical evaluation finds that the method consistently and significantly outperforms the compared alternatives, including a broad range of kernels. The contribution is an expressive feature representation with efficient computation, supported by strong results in the evaluated settings. Its regional modeling and treatment of feature pairs provide the mechanism for using nonlinear structure with linear learning algorithms.
icml-2013-the-pairwise-piecewise-linear-.tldr: A feature map based on discretization and interpolation combines efficient linear learning with strong nonlinear classification results.
